entities.name: Eudes Rigaud
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Eudes Rigaud, also known as Odo Rigaud, was a towering figure in the French ecclesiastical hierarchy of the High Middle Ages, serving as the Archbishop of Rouen from 1247 until his death on July 9, 1275. A distinguished Franciscan friar and former university lecturer, Rigaud stood at the intersection of religious reform, intellectual life, and political power during the reign of King Louis IX of France. His extensive pastoral visitations across the vast Archdiocese of Rouen, meticulously documented in his register, provide an unparalleled window into the social, economic, and spiritual conditions of thirteenth-century Norman society, making him a crucial source for understanding medieval church administration and daily life.

Born into the minor nobility of Brie, Rigaud joined the Franciscan order in Paris around 1236, quickly distinguishing himself as a master of theology at the University of Paris. His intellectual prowess and commitment to mendicant ideals led to his appointment as the first Franciscan regent master at the university in 1242 and later as provincial minister of the Franciscan province of France. King Louis IX, recognizing Rigaud's administrative and spiritual acumen, personally nominated him for the archbishopric of Rouen, a strategically vital see in Normandy. Throughout his archiepiscopate, Rigaud conducted rigorous and detailed visitations of hundreds of parishes, monasteries, and convents, recording observations on clerical conduct, monastic discipline, and the material state of church properties in his invaluable *Registrum Visitationum*.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Eudes Rigaud's meticulous *Registrum Visitationum* provides an unparalleled, granular record of medieval church life, offering historians unique insights into 13th-century ecclesiastical administration and societal conditions. His work directly informed and influenced the reform efforts of the French Church, particularly in Normandy, during the High Middle Ages.
